extracted.intended_audience: CVPR 2026 paper reviewers (conference peer reviewers in computer vision)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for reviewers of CVPR 2026 submissions: how to read, assess, write reviews, handle rebuttals/discussions, follow ethics/LLM policies, and make well-justified final recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the best decisions to serve the community: be fair, thoughtful, consistent, and transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals include fairness, thoughtfulness, consistency, and transparent reasoning so authors can see why decisions were made. Keep policies clear to minimize confusion, frustration, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role: recommendations vs decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers provide well-reasoned recommendations to help Area Chairs decide; reviewers do not make final acceptance decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should help decision-makers understand merits and weaknesses and give constructive feedback to authors. Use skill, judgment, and experience; write reviews that clearly explain reasoning; respond to rebuttals fairly and on time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional objectivity and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus evaluation on the work itself, not assumptions about the authors; treat everyone with fairness, compassion, and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support opinions with evidence, avoid inventing policies, and maintain professional objectivity. Report improprieties via proper channels and avoid conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance criteria (what should be accepted?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend acceptance for papers that will interest CVPR attendees, are technically sound, and contribute meaningfully (methodologically, empirically, or conceptually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance novelty with significance and potential impact. Consider reproducibility, data contribution, ethical data use, societal impact, and discussion of limitations. Minor fixable issues should not drive rejection. Scope judgments should be cautious; if truly out of scope, explain and suggest better venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper does not need to be perfect to be accepted; it must advance the field and meet quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor, fixable issues should not be the basis for rejection. Emphasize fundamental soundness and contribution over small problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible and timely reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews must be specific, accurate, original (not LLM-generated), and submitted on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irresponsible reviews include short/generic text not tied to the paper, factual errors indicating superficial reading, and content generated or substantially assisted by LLMs. Late or irresponsible reviews may trigger consequences including desk rejection for papers on which the reviewer is an author. Follow the Responsible Reviewing Policy and Reviewing Deadline Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect anonymity and confidentiality of submissions and do not reuse or build on ideas from submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect double-blind review and avoid author-identity searches. Declare and avoid conflicts of interest promptly. Handle human subjects and personal data with heightened scrutiny. Never discuss submissions outside the review process. Destroy materials after the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM usage policy for reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) must not be used to generate, translate, paraphrase, or otherwise compose review content or to process submission content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted: non-confidential background research on publicly available concepts/methods (not the submission itself); grammar checks of short phrases you have already written (under ~50 words, containing no submission-specific content). Prohibited: inputting any text, figures, or content from the submission into an LLM; using LLMs to summarize, paraphrase, analyze the paper, or draft any portion of your review; using LLMs to translate the paper or your review. Violations may result in a two-year submission ban; report suspected prompt injection to AC/PCs immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reviewing, inspect your assigned stack for conflicts and suitability and plan your time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate effort based on each paper’s complexity and scope. Inform your AC immediately if reassignment is needed. Review relevant policies and guidelines. If you suspect a policy violation, alert Chairs but continue to review the paper as if no violation occurred (they will investigate separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Careful reading and short summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper thoroughly and draft a short (2-4 sentence) accurate summary in your own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary helps reveal gaps in understanding—if you can't summarize clearly, read again. Assess correctness, completeness, clarity of contribution, and positioning versus prior work. Identify the paper's core claims and evaluate the evidence supporting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3 — Required review components
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should include a concise summary, strengths, weaknesses, constructive suggestions, and a justified recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengths and weaknesses must be specific and evidence-based. Justify your recommendation by clearly connecting assessment to rating. Back 'done before' claims with references and explain relationships to prior work. Do not over-weight SOTA tables alone—consider experimental design, insights, and broader contributions. Keep tone professional; avoid second-person address; be specific and concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on single metrics or SOTA tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate quality solely with leaderboard results or SOTA numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider experimental design, analysis, ablations, insights, and broader contribution; check whether gains arise from confounds like more training data or other non-algorithmic factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and wording conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use professional tone; avoid second-person addressing ('you' or 'the authors'); refer to 'the paper'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific and concrete. Avoid vague praise or vague criticism. Keep language constructive and evidence-based; avoid sarcasm or dismissive tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reviewing pitfalls and correction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid standard errors such as ignorance/inaccuracy, pure opinion, novelty fallacy, blank assertions, policy entrepreneurism, and intellectual laziness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each: (1) Ignorance/Inaccuracy — do not state technical claims without justification; point to specific lines/assumptions and request clarification. (2) Pure Opinion — avoid unsupported subjective claims; anchor relevance to concrete aspects. (3) Novelty Fallacy — novelty alone doesn't guarantee quality; evaluate empirical/theoretical contributions. (4) Blank Assertions — cite prior work if claiming 'done before'. (5) Policy Entrepreneurism — do not invent acceptance rules (e.g., 'must release code'). (6) Intellectual Laziness — don't equate SOTA result with accept or lack of SOTA with reject; analyze causes of performance differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for standard errors to check in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalizing a review, check for ignorance/inaccuracy, pure opinion, novelty fallacy, blank assertions, policy entrepreneurism, and intellectual laziness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples to replace vague or incorrect statements. Request clarifications, cite evidence, and avoid inventing policy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4 — Rebuttal and discussion engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Read rebuttals carefully, engage substantively, and update ratings if concerns are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what changed your mind and why. Do not demand substantial new experiments during rebuttal; small, reasonable checks are acceptable. Focus rebuttal engagement on clarifications and addressing misunderstandings rather than requiring new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5 — Finalization and final justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in AC-reviewer discussions, ensure your reasoning is clear to the AC, and submit a well-justified final recommendation by the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final justifications must be specific, evidence-based, and clearly connected to your rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unacceptable final justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid generic or vague final statements, contradictory or unsupported logic, and unexplained changes after rebuttal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of unacceptable statements include 'The paper is good overall' or 'I don't feel excited about it.' Avoid concluding reject after claiming technical soundness without explaining the contradiction. If changing a score after rebuttal, explain which concerns were addressed and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of strong/weak/borderline/reject justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Model language for final justifications across decision categories shows how to tie assessment to evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good examples show concrete contributions, theoretical/empirical support, ablations, and how rebuttal affected evaluation. Weak/borderline examples show limited datasets or missing comparisons and explain residual uncertainty. Reject examples identify fundamental technical issues and missing evidence where rebuttal failed to address problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities to the Area Chair (AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear, well-reasoned recommendations; explain evidence; read rebuttals; participate in discussions; and respond promptly to AC queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag concerns about policy violations or ethical issues immediately and cooperate with AC instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: What reviewers can expect from ACs
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs will help resolve conflicts/assignments, offer guidance on policy questions, coordinate with SACs/PCs for serious issues, and support reviewers if struggling with out-of-expertise papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your AC early for reassignment or policy questions; ACs provide escalation channels for serious problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication norms with ACs
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact AC early if you need reassignment or have concerns; be responsive during discussion phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember the AC knows reviewer identity; sloppy or irresponsible reviews reflect poorly and may affect future reviewing opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final review checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submission, verify summary presence, standard errors check, incorrect mathematics, omitted material, strengths/weaknesses with evidence, review length, tone, policy compliance, and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure concise accurate summary is present; check for omitted experiments, missing citations, or incorrect derivations; make sure strengths/weaknesses are evidence-backed; maintain professional tone; comply with LLM, confidentiality, and conflict policies; submit before the deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to escalate (immediate alert to AC/SAC/PC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately report suspected plagiarism/self-plagiarism, dual submission, unethical data use/privacy violations, fabricated/falsified results, violation of withdrawn-dataset norms, prompt injection/LLM abuse, or human-subjects protocol violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not investigate independently. Report concerns to the AC who will coordinate further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation guidance (FAQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended time per paper is about 4–6 hours in total, but this varies by complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical breakdown: 1–2 hours reading, 2–3 hours writing the review, and 1–2 hours for rebuttal response and discussion. Adjust based on paper difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling out-of-expertise assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: If assigned a paper well outside your expertise, contact your AC immediately and clearly state your expertise limitations in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can still review if comfortable; AC may assign an additional reviewer with more specific expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on searching for author identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not search for or attempt to discover authors' identities to assess credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This violates double-blind review; assess the work on its own merits. If you inadvertently learn identities, avoid letting it bias your review and report any anonymity violations to the AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling anonymity violations in submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a submission violates anonymity (includes identifying information), report it to your AC but continue to review the work itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AC and PCs will decide whether the violation warrants action; do not let the violation derail your substantive assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encountering arXiv or public versions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find a submission on arXiv or elsewhere naturally, do not let venue or reception bias your review; do not actively search for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may come across public versions but avoid using that to judge the submission's acceptability beyond what is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating rebuttals that promise future fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess rebuttals based on what they actually demonstrate, not promises about future camera-ready fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises without evidence should not change your assessment; accept only indicated clarifications or evidence presented in the rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreements with other reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreement is normal; explain your perspective and reasoning and engage constructively in discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about evidence and rationale, and participate in AC-mediated discussion to help synthesize viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted narrow LLM uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitted LLM uses are limited to non-confidential background research on public concepts and grammar checks of short phrases already written (< ~50 words) with no submission-specific content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not input submission text into LLMs; do not use LLMs to summarize/analyze/translate submission or draft review text. Report prompt injection if suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dos and Don'ts summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise actionable list: DO ground judgments in evidence, be specific and constructive, engage with rebuttals, flag conflicts, respect confidentiality, and meet deadlines; DON'T use LLMs to generate/analyze review content, share submission content, search for authors, invent policies, make unsupported assertions, or submit generic/superficial reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the DO list during the review lifecycle and avoid all items in the DON'T list. These are quick heuristics to maintain quality and integrity.
